designs.live_title: The Last Star: What Happens When a Red Dwarf Dies?
designs.live_description:
The last star in the universe will be a red dwarf. This is what happens when it dies — and why black dwarfs are what remains.

Orbit rides deep time to the last star in the universe — and asks what remains when even that light fails.

Heat death explained without dreadbait: why stars stop being born, why red dwarfs outlive the Sun, and what "the end" actually means in physics. Real observations, honest uncertainty, and wonder without fearbait.

Chapters
0:00 — The Last Light
1:08 — When Stars Stop Being Born
2:34 — The Age of Red Dwarfs
4:17 — When the Last Star Dies
6:47 — What Remains
8:15 — Keep Looking

If you enjoy calm investigations into the biggest mysteries in the universe, subscribe to Orbit With Ben.

If you want to go further

A film can open a question. A good book sits with the uncertainty longer. The End of Everything, Katie Mack's look at how the universe might close, is the one I'd keep on the desk after this episode.

designs.live_title: What Happens During the Milky Way Andromeda Collision?
designs.live_description:
The Milky Way Andromeda collision: in about 4 billion years, the Andromeda galaxy fills our sky — and the galaxies don't smash into fireworks.

Andromeda is already inbound. This film walks the honest clock, the night sky rewriting, why stars almost never hit, whether Earth survives the crash, and what one merged galaxy looks like after.

designs.title_B_proposal: How Long Do Moons, Rings and Stars Last?
designs.status: draft; no test armed; Chief and panel required
designs.live_title: How Long Will Anything in Space Last?
designs.live_description:
Nothing you can see in the night sky is permanent — from Saturn's ice rings raining into the planet right now to the last red dwarf stars shining ten trillion years from now. How long does each of them have left?

This full-length countdown walks five clocks across the universe, from the shortest to the longest: Saturn's vanishing rings (100 to 300 million years), the Moon slowly drifting away from Earth at 3.8 cm a year and ending the window of perfect total solar eclipses, the Milky Way's future collision with Andromeda billions of years from now, the ultra-dense neutron stars left behind when giant stars explode, and the quiet red dwarfs that will outlive every other star in the cosmos.

Chapters
0:00 Nothing in the sky is permanent
0:53 The Rings Are Leaving
10:12 The Moon Lets Go
18:47 Two Galaxies Meet
29:19 What Dead Stars Leave
39:04 The Last Light
